svg.title: Layer 3 policy needs the traffic to traverse the policy device; traffic inside one VLAN never does, so the VLAN boundary is the smallest security domain
svg.desc: Left: a switch holding PC-A and PC-B in VLAN 10, uplinked to a gateway/firewall where the policy lives. The path from PC-A to PC-B is switched inside the box and never reaches the policy device, which is the physical basis of lateral movement. The path from PC-A to a server in another VLAN is routed and therefore inspected. Right: the trust domain arithmetic - a VLAN of 500 devices in which 499 do not trust each other is one trust domain of 500, and no firewall rule anywhere in the network changes that. Bottom: three conclusions - size the VLAN by trust, not by floor or cable run; if a VLAN must carry mixed trust, add in-switch controls (private VLAN, SGT, 802.1X, DAI) because no router on the path can help; and treat every VLAN as a security domain in the design document, with an owner and a trust level.
svg.text: Why Layer 2 is the last blind spot: the policy device is only in the path of Layer 3
Firewalls, ACLs, uRPF and route policy share one premise - the traffic must traverse the box. Same-VLAN traffic never does
WHERE THE POLICY PHYSICALLY SITS
Gateway / FW
ACL · zone policy · uRPF
policy lives here
L2 switch
VLAN 10 · access layer
trunk
PC-A
PC-B
①
① PC-A → PC-B: switched inside the box. No router, no firewall, no ACL - every Layer 3 control is bypassed.
② PC-A → a server in another VLAN: routed through the gateway and therefore inspected - this half works.
THE TRUST DOMAIN ARITHMETIC
One VLAN = one trust domain, whether you meant it or not
A single VLAN with 500 endpoints, 499 of which do not trust each other
= 500 devices in one trust boundary. The design has already failed.
Flat VLAN 10 - one boundary, one policy, no interior controls
500 endpoints · free lateral movement
Split by trust - five boundaries, five policies, five owners
100 endpoints each · every crossing is now a routed, inspectable hop
The boundary is set by the switch, so the design lever is where you cut the VLANs -
not how many firewall rules you write above them.
THREE CONCLUSIONS FOR THE DESIGN DOCUMENT

g.text: Not by floor, cable run or switch port
count. Two endpoints that must not
reach each other belong to two VLANs
Then the control has to live inside the
No router on the path can help you
Trust level, owner, allowed peers and
review date - the same four fields you
would demand for a firewall zone

svg.text: The VLAN is not a convenience for broadcast containment. In a security design it is the smallest unit of trust, and everything above it is only as strong as this cut.
